name: Pedro Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 27 and supervise five clerks handling travel insurance claims and policy changes. I have a bachelor’s degree, earn typical pay for this job and use AI every day to group receipts, but I check the dates and cover myself. I rent a small flat alone, have no children and have saved roughly three months of expenses. There are some other insurers nearby, though a vacancy is not the same as an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my team that the receipt sorter saves us a few minutes, not the whole claims job. I would still ask each clerk to read the policy date before sending a rejection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My current pay and three months saved make the rent manageable, and our supervisor has not talked about cuts. A tidy travel claim can still have the wrong date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my Friday check of ten rejected travel claims and put 80 a month into savings while my hours hold. In the first year I would use the same receipt tool and check its mistakes against the policy schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own work and bills in this picture. The missed dates still irritate me more than the software itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which mistake sticks with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A family sent a boarding pass dated the day after its policy ended. The tool grouped the pass neatly, and I had to explain why a tidy file was not covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you show a junior clerk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the team the wrong date without putting the family’s name on a shared screen. No one learns from a mystery error.

say: I would keep **policy dates** in human review.
I would use the **daily receipt sorter** for routine filing.
think: I have **three months saved** and current paid hours.
I know a **tidy file** can still produce a wrong rejection.
do: **Check ten rejected claims** each Friday against the dates printed on each travel policy.
**Save 80 monthly** while my current paid hours continue and the rent stays covered.
S0.quote: A tidy travel claim can still have the wrong date.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** groups receipts, while he personally checks cover dates.
His **current wages and savings** support a calm baseline without guaranteeing future work.

steps.text: Check ten rejected travel claims every Friday against policy dates
Save 80 monthly while current paid hours continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say Steady Disruption could let software write replies and check ordinary travel claims before a clerk sees them. I would ask our staff association to see the error figures and the paid hours behind any new target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own team lead hours could be cut if one person watches several automated queues. Three months of expenses buys some time, but it cannot replace a wage for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would run a small test on invented travel claims and record which policy dates the tool misses. I would take the results to the staff association and ask for paid review hours; if my hours actually fall, I would check real local claims vacancies and their wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my hours even while I want to test the tool. I do not want an error report used as a reason to leave one clerk with three queues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the association ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The association could ask who signs a rejection and how many paid hours remain for appeals. I can supply the test results, but I cannot promise the company will agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would only apply if a posted job pays enough for rent, food and travel. An opening at another insurer may use the same software and cut staff too.

say: I would demand **error figures** and paid review hours.
I would test **invented travel claims** before using real records.
think: I could lose **paid lead hours** if one clerk watches several automated claim queues.
I cannot treat **three months saved** as a replacement for my wage.
do: **Test invented claims** this month and record missed policy dates.
**Bring findings** to the staff association for a paid-hours request.
**Check posted local jobs** if hours fall and wages cover essentials.
S1.quote: I do not want an error report used as a reason to leave one clerk with three queues.
fieldNote: His **test is concrete**, but a staffing concession is only a request.
The **local job search** starts if paid hours fall and requires bill-covering wages.

steps.text: Test invented travel claims and bring missed dates to association for paid review hours
Check posted local claims vacancies if hours fall and wages cover essentials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that full AGI by 2028 could read policies, check receipts and answer customers more cheaply than us. Robots handling luggage or visiting damaged property may follow around 2031, but our desk work faces the earlier date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my claims lead job to disappear, and I have been lying awake thinking about the rent. Three months saved is a landing strip, not a new job. I cannot count on someone else paying my bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask for written notice of any team cuts and stop the 80 monthly saving target if hours fall, keeping the cash for rent. If the job ends in the first year after 2028, I would apply only to actual paid local customer appeals openings that cover my basic bills and ask the public employment office about my eligibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed, even though I like the technology. My rent arrives every month whether a claims queue has a person attached or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would appeals work last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot say appeals jobs will survive the same AGI that handles claims. I would ask for the job duties and written pay before spending the buffer on travel to an interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you accept an offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need an offer with paid hours and enough income for rent and food. A training promise without paid work would not carry me through the fourth month.

say: I would warn that **claims desk work** faces AGI by 2028.
I would separate **later robots** from the earlier loss of thinking tasks.
think: I expect my **lead job to end** and lie awake over rent.
I cannot assume **appeals vacancies** survive AGI.
do: **Request written cut notice** now and hold savings for rent.
Apply to **paid appeals jobs** after loss only if wages cover essentials.
S2.quote: Three months saved is a landing strip, not a new job.
fieldNote: He expects **major wage loss** in 2028 and reports broken sleep.
A **paid appeals opening** must exist and cover bills; public support depends on eligibility.

steps.text: Request written team-cut notice and preserve three-month rent reserve
Apply for actual paid local appeals openings after 2028 loss if wages cover bills
Ask public employment office about eligibility if displaced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team that AGI by 2031 gives us several years to test decisions and demand a proper appeal route. Robots doing physical work may come around 2034, but claim reading and replies change first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could use those years to move from sorting files to checking how decisions are explained, though AGI may do that as well. I would not pay for a diploma on the hope of a job that has not been advertised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the insurer for a paid six-week trial checking invented denial letters against policy wording, with my current hours protected in writing. If they approve it, I would keep a weekly error log; after 2031, if my role ends, I would seek an actual paid local appeals post only where the trial meets its stated requirements and pay covers my bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the eventual wage risk but more able to act with five years. A paid trial would tell me whether this is a job or just a course title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the trial been approved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My supervisor has not approved the trial or protected hours yet. If the answer is no, I would stay on my paid claims rota and keep saving rather than leave for unpaid practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trial qualify you for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to see a job notice saying what training and experience it requires. Six weeks of practice might help, but it is not a professional qualification.

say: I would seek a **paid trial** before AGI reaches claims in 2031.
I would insist on **written hours protection** for the trial.
think: I could build **appeal checking skill** but still face AGI.
I cannot treat **six weeks** as a qualification.
do: **Request a paid trial** with current hours protected in writing.
**Log denial-letter errors** weekly only if the trial is approved.
**Seek paid appeals work** after loss only if qualified and bills are covered.
feel: **Anxious** about later income, with a conditional plan.
S3.quote: A paid trial would tell me whether this is a job or just a course title.
fieldNote: The **six-week trial needs approval** and written protection of existing pay and hours before he can join it.
A later **appeals vacancy** needs real demand, matching requirements and bill-covering wages after AGI arrives.

steps.text: Request paid six-week denial-review trial with written protection of current hours
Log invented denial-letter errors weekly if trial is approved
Seek qualified paid local appeals vacancy after 2031 loss if wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to demand clear denial records and build a reserve. Robots doing physical inspection could arrive around 2039, after the claims desk changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel secure in my current hours for the next few years, yet I am 27 and cannot build a whole working life on one claims title. I would use the time to find out what paid work actually remains instead of buying a string of certificates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the Friday rejected-claim checks and ask the staff association for an annual count of paid appeal posts. I would save 100 monthly while wages hold; if my role ends after 2036, I would apply to actual local posts only when I meet the requirements and the pay covers rent and essentials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the long end of that decade, but I can pay this year’s rent and plan. A ten-year warning is useful only if the pay slips keep coming while I prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the annual count show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how many appeals were reversed by a person and how many paid clerks handled them. An annual count would show whether a new job route is growing or closing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not move on a rumour about work in another city. I would need a real offer and a budget before changing my flat or leaving the current job.

say: I would seek **annual paid-post counts** through the staff association before AGI reaches claims in 2036.
I would keep **human appeal records** visible so claimants can challenge wrong decisions.
think: I feel **secure for now** with current hours and three months saved.
I need **paid work later** if the claims role ends.
do: **Keep Friday claim checks** while the present role pays.
**Request annual staffing counts** through the association.
**Save 100 monthly** while wages hold; seek qualified paid vacancies after loss.
feel: **Uneasy** about later work, secure for the next few years.
S4.quote: A ten-year warning is useful only if the pay slips keep coming while I prepare.
fieldNote: The **longer runway** supports savings and evidence gathering without making later work certain.
His **future applications** require real qualified openings with enough pay for basic bills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect the paid claims job to disappear before I can build another skill. Written notice, a real bill-covering offer and confirmed temporary support eligibility would help me keep the flat while I look.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a rejection can be appealed by a person who understands the policy. I would rather see one named appeals clerk than a perfect-looking dashboard.

headlineQuote: I would rather see one named appeals clerk than a perfect-looking dashboard.
portrait: Pedro is a **27-year-old claims lead** with a bachelor’s degree, typical pay and three months saved.
He rents **alone**, has no children and checks travel policy dates after using AI daily.
He wants **test evidence** and paid review hours before automation sets staffing targets.
He expects **2028 job loss**, but uses the longer scenarios to seek funded practice and real vacancies.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his claims wage before he has another paid skill.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a bill-covering job offer and confirmed temporary support eligibility would help.
